title: Long Island Museum
summary: Enduring Heart brings Native history and contemporary art to Stony Brook, August 20–December 20, 2026. Explore the museum’s connections to Shinnecock decoy carving, Native storytelling, and living cultural traditions.

why_this_matters: The story of a decoy changes when its maker is named. Research on the Herrick decoys connects museum objects with Shinnecock artist Charles Sumner Bunn, while Enduring Heart gives contemporary Native artists room to tell their own stories. Together, these histories invite visitors to look at both the object and the person whose knowledge shaped it.
introduction_title: Enduring Heart: Native American Long Island
introduction_content:
August 20–December 20, 2026 · LIM Art Museum

Enduring Heart brings historical objects and contemporary Native art into conversation. Developed with an advisory panel of Native community members and scholars, it features work by Tecumseh Ceaser, Jeremy Dennis, David Bunn Martine, Lydia Ann Wallace-Chavez, and other artists.[1]

Dennis’s participating photographs include Arrow Head Collector (2018), Land Claim (2019), and Many Nations, Under One, All Invisible (2025). His staged images invite viewers to consider Native identity, land, and the ways American history is pictured.[2]
history_title: Native artists, collections, and community voices
history_content:
Shinnecock carving and the decoy collection

The museum opened The Bayman’s Art decoy gallery on June 17, 2000. Its later exhibition Eugene Cuffee, Shinnecock Carver, June 21–August 15, 2003, brought Shinnecock carving into its exhibition program.[3]

The Herrick decoys also connect the museum to research on Shinnecock carver Charles Sumner Bunn. Researcher Jamie Reason describes a 2005 meeting at the museum with curator Joshua Ruff, Orson Munn Jr., Donal O’Brien, and Joe Jannsen, during which Munn compared the Herrick shorebirds with his family’s decoys. Reason’s account documents the effort to revisit objects long attributed to “Bowman” and restore Bunn’s name to their history.[4]

Read Duck Decoys for the wider story of Native makers, family knowledge, and changing attributions. The collection’s history offers a question to carry into any museum: whose name is attached to an object, and whose knowledge made it possible?

Community members telling their own stories

On November 16, 2025, Telling our Story: Long Island’s Native American Heritage brought members of the Matinecock, Montaukett, Setalcott, Shinnecock, and Unkechaug Nations into the museum’s public program. Montaukett dancers performed; Madeline “Mandy” Jackson moderated, with Helen Sells and Sandi Brewster-walker among the speakers.[5]

The 2026 exhibition continues these relationships. Its advisory committee includes Sandi Brewster-walker, Jeremy Dennis, David Bunn Martine, Helen Sells, Chief Harry Wallace, Allison McGovern, Lorrie McCallister, and Joseph M. Pierce.[1]

Mishoons and living waterway traditions

The museum’s August 20, 2026 program with Shinnecock cultural leader Chenae Bullock explored the revival of mishoons—dugout canoes—and the community knowledge carried through their making and use. The museum moved this program online as a free virtual event.[6]

Learn with the exhibition

October 27, 2026, 4–6:30 p.m.: the museum’s Smithsonian National Youth Summit combines discussion, an interactive Enduring Heart tour, and an artist-led workshop for teen leaders ages 14–18. The posted application deadline is September 17; use the museum’s registration page for availability.[7]

November 21, 2026, 1–2 p.m.: the Boys & Girls Club of the Shinnecock Indian Nation Dance Troupe is scheduled to share powwow-style and traditional Shinnecock dances. The museum lists the program as included with admission.[8]
whereintheworld_content: The Long Island Museum of American Art, History and Carriages is at 1200 Route 25A, Stony Brook, NY 11790, within the map’s Setauket ancestral landscape. Check the museum website for current opening hours, admission, access information, and program reservations. Exhibition dates describe the run of the show; the museum is not open every day.[9]
